R071-01.notes: Passage frames David vs. Liebowitz/Margolis on what QWERTY's survival shows. A overstates (author is neutral); C covers only paragraph 1 background; D is unsupported. Facts checked: Sholes & Glidden machine sold by Remington from 1874, typebar-jam and telegraph-operator (Yasuoka) explanations, David 1985 AER 'Clio and the Economics of QWERTY', Dvorak patent granted 1936 with vowels/common letters on home (middle) row, 1944 Navy study, Liebowitz & Margolis 1990 'Fable of the Keys' noting Dvorak's role and the 1956 Strong/GSA study -- all accurate as hedged.

R071-02.notes: Direct detail. D is a trap twisting the telegraph-operator alternative (needs of operators, not signal order; and it is not the 'popular' explanation). B describes Dvorak's layout.

R071-03.notes: Paraphrases the definition given right after the term. B/C/D have no support.

R071-04.notes: Paragraph 3 rebuts David's Navy-study evidence. A wrong (jamming is paragraph 1); B, C unsupported (passage never says Navy adopted Dvorak).

R071-05.notes: Conflict of interest: Dvorak directed it and stood to profit. The 1950s contradicting study is a separate point but is not among options; D wrongly attributes experiments to David. 'Mainly' is acceptable since A is the only reason about the study itself listed.

R071-06.notes: Contrapositive of 'If no clearly superior layout had been available ... not evidence.' D is the strongest trap (a different director would not itself establish a superior layout). 'Only if' reading is logically valid.

R071-07.notes: A misassigns the origin explanations (neither party is tied to them); C reverses evidence use; D uses extreme 'always/never' that neither side claims.

R071-08.notes: 'Both lessons may be worth keeping' plus the two-sided 'does not prove' sentence. C is the main trap but author says the question is hard to settle.

R071-09.notes: Final sentence: evidence 'tangled up with the interests of the people who collected it.' D (lost records) is plausible-sounding but unstated.

R071-10.notes: A 'pointed reply' that challenges David's evidence = sharply critical. B literal sense; C, D not fitting. 'Deliberately brief' has slight lure but nothing supports brevity.
